entry: Swedish chemist, one of the founders of modern chemistry. Berzelius began as a physician, but his lasting work lay in [[Electrochemistry|electrochemistry]] and [[Stoichiometry|stoichiometry]], the quantitative relations between elements in compounds and reactions. He determined many atomic weights, articulated the "Law of Constant Proportions" and developed improved methods of chemical analysis. He is credited with discovering [[Cerium]] and [[Selenium]] and with being the first to isolate [[Silicon]] and [[Thorium]]. He devised a system of chemical notation that showed the composition of compounds both qualitatively and quantitatively, using abbreviations and superscripts for atom counts. He also developed electrochemical dualism, the theory that compounds are oxide salts held together by electrostatic interactions, which came to be seen as insufficient. He is known in Sweden as the "Father of Swedish Chemistry."

Japanese popular music genre that entered the mainstream in the 1990s. Its roots lie in traditional Japanese music and global 1960s pop and rock. The term replaced *kayōkyoku* ("Lyric Singing Music"), the name for Japanese popular music from the 1920s to the 1980s. Japanese rock bands such as Happy End fused [[The Beatles|Beatles]]-style rock with Japanese music in the 1960s and 1970s, and new wave acts such as Yellow Magic Orchestra shaped the genre in the late 1970s. Subgenres include city pop, technopop, J-Euro and Shibuya-kei. The term was first applied only to Western-style musicians, but it became a blanket term covering many other genres, including much of the 1990s [[Rock music|rock]] scene. In 1990 the Japanese subsidiary of Tower Records defined J-pop as all Japanese music belonging to the Recording Industry Association of Japan except independent music.

German philosopher and social theorist in the tradition of critical theory and pragmatism. His work addressed communicative rationality and the public sphere, and he held professorships at [[Heidelberg University]] and Goethe University Frankfurt. His early book *The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere* (1962) was a social history of the emergence and decline of bourgeois public discourse. *The Theory of Communicative Action* (1981) advanced a theory of rationality grounded in interpersonal linguistic communication. He developed the concept of discourse ethics and argued that the Enlightenment was an "unfinished project" requiring correction rather than abandonment. In the West German *Historikerstreit* of 1986 he accused conservative historians of relativizing the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]]. In a 2004 dialogue with Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, later [[Pope Benedict XVI]], he addressed religion in secular societies. He also directed the Max Planck Institute in Starnberg.

Polish statesman and first Marshal of Poland (from 1920). He served as Chief of State from November 1918, when Poland regained its independence, until 1922. Early in his career he led the Polish Socialist Party and formed the Polish Legions, which fought alongside [[Austria-Hungary]] against Russia in [[World War I]]. From 1919 to 1921 he commanded Polish forces in six wars that redefined the country's borders. In August 1920 his forces repelled the Soviet invasion at the Battle of Warsaw during the [[Polish–Soviet War]]. He retired from active politics in 1923 but returned to power in the May Coup of 1926 and became the strongman of the Sanation government, focusing on military and foreign affairs. Supporters credit him with founding modern Poland; critics cite authoritarian tendencies and the imprisonment of political opponents at Bereza Kartuska.

Muslim scholar and jurist, the sixth Shia imam. He was the eponymous founder of the Ja'fari school of [[Fiqh|Islamic jurisprudence]]. More traditions are cited from him in the canonical Twelver [[Hadith|hadith]] collections than from all other Imams combined, though their attribution to him is questionable. Doctrines ascribed to him include *nass*, the divinely inspired designation of each Imam by the previous one, and *taqiya*, religious dissimulation under persecution. Sunni Muslims revere him as a reliable transmitter of hadith, and he transmitted to the Sunni scholars [[Abu Hanifa]] and [[Malik ibn Anas]], namesakes of the Hanafi and Maliki schools. He kept aloof from the political conflicts of his time, and Shia sources say he was poisoned at the instigation of the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur. After his death one group followed his eldest son, forming the Isma'ili branch, while the larger Ja'fari, or Twelver, group accepted the Imamate of his younger son, Musa al-Kazim.

Purported author of a large corpus of Arabic writings, known in Latin as Geber. The approximately 215 surviving treatises mainly deal with [[Alchemy|alchemy]] and chemistry, magic and Shi'ite religious philosophy, though the original scope covered cosmology, astronomy, medicine and logic. Works attributed to him, tentatively dated to c. 850–c. 950, contain the oldest known systematic classification of chemical substances and the oldest known instructions for making [[Ammonium chloride|sal ammoniac]] from organic substances. They also contain one of the earliest versions of the sulfur-mercury theory of metals, which remained dominant until the 18th century. Much of the writing concerns "the science of the balance," which aimed to reduce phenomena to measures and quantitative proportions. Modern scholars doubt that a historical Jabir existed; he is generally thought to be a pseudonym for an anonymous school of Shi'ite alchemists of the late 9th and early 10th centuries.

[[New Zealand]] politician, prime minister and Labour Party leader from 2017 to 2023. Ardern led a coalition government with New Zealand First, supported by the Green Party, and at 37 became the world's youngest female [[Head of government|head of government]]. After the [[Christchurch mosque shootings]] in 2019 she rapidly introduced strict gun laws. Her government's COVID-19 response was praised for containing the virus. Labour won an overall majority of 65 seats in the October 2020 general election. In January 2023 she resigned as leader, stating that she did not have "enough in the tank."

American actor, comedian and musician. He starred in family and comedy films and voiced [[Animation|animated]] features, including Po in the *Kung Fu Panda* franchise from 2008. He became a leading man in *School of Rock* (2003) and was critically praised for portraying Bernie Tiede in *Bernie* (2011). He also voiced Bowser in *The Super Mario Bros. Movie* (2023). With Kyle Gass he formed the comedy musical duo Tenacious D in 1994; the duo has won one Grammy. Since 2018 he has run a YouTube channel called *Jablinski Games*.

American novelist and poet, a pioneer of the Beat Generation. Of French-Canadian parentage, he grew up in a French-speaking home in Lowell, Massachusetts, and learned English at about age six. He served as a United States Merchant Mariner during [[World War II]]. His first published book was *The Town and the City* (1950), and *On the Road* (1957) made him a Beat icon. He went on to publish 12 more novels and numerous volumes of poetry. Known for spontaneous, stream-of-consciousness prose, he wrote about religion, [[Mysticism|mysticism]], [[Buddhism]] and life in [[New York City]] and the San Francisco Bay Area. He became an underground celebrity and a progenitor of the hippie movement, although he despised the hippies. Several previously unseen works were published after his death, and he influenced [[Bob Dylan]], the [[The Beatles|Beatles]] and [[The Doors|the Doors]].

American [[Electrical engineering|electrical engineer]], co-inventor of the [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuit]]. While working at Texas Instruments in 1958, he concluded that components could be made en masse in a single piece of [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] material, solving the "tyranny of numbers" in circuit design. He demonstrated a working device on September 12, 1958. His patent for the first integrated circuit, which placed different components on one substrate, was filed in 1959. Robert Noyce of Fairchild Semiconductor independently made a similar circuit a few months later, and the two are generally credited as co-inventors. For this invention Kilby shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics. He was also a co-inventor of the handheld calculator and the thermal printer. Earlier, at Centralab, he worked on [[Germanium|germanium]] [[Transistor|transistors]] for hearing aids. He later pioneered military and commercial applications of microchips.

American [[Comic book|comic book]] artist, one of the medium's major innovators. In 1940 he and writer-editor Joe Simon created [[Captain America]] for Timely Comics, a predecessor of [[Marvel Comics]]. In the 1960s he co-created many of Marvel's major characters, including the Avengers, the Fantastic Four, the [[Hulk]], [[Iron Man]], Thor and the [[X-Men]]. Dissatisfied with authorship credit and creators' rights, he left Marvel in 1970 for [[DC Comics]], where he created the Fourth World saga, whose New Gods remain part of the DC Universe. In 1987 he was one of three inaugural inductees of the Will Eisner Comic Book Hall of Fame. In 2017 he was posthumously named a Disney Legend, as his creations formed the basis of the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]]. Fans call him "The King."

Canadian-born American [[Film|film]] executive and president of Warner Bros. Studios. His career spanned more than 55 years. With his brother Sam Warner he procured the technology for the film industry's first talking picture, *The Jazz Singer* (1927). After Sam's death he clashed with his brothers Harry and Albert, and in the 1950s he secretly purchased their shares to gain control. He recruited many of the studio's top stars and promoted the hard-edged social dramas for which it became known. A staunch Republican, he nonetheless encouraged films that promoted the policies of Democratic President [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]]. He opposed [[Fascism|fascism]] and criticized [[Nazi Germany]] before the U.S. entered World War II. After the war he testified as a friendly witness before the House Un-American Activities Committee, naming screenwriters suspected of [[Communism|communism]]. Employees feared him, but he earned respect for his shrewd instincts.

American actor noted for both comic and dramatic roles. He won Academy Awards for *Mister Roberts* (1955) and *Save the Tiger* (1973), and was nominated for *Some Like It Hot* (1959) and *The Apartment* (1960), both directed by [[Billy Wilder]]. He won a Primetime Emmy for *Tuesdays with Morrie* (1999). His long collaboration with [[Walter Matthau]] produced ten films between 1966 and 1998, including *The Odd Couple* (1968). *The Guardian* called him "the most successful tragi-comedian of his age."

American novelist, journalist and activist. A pioneer of commercial fiction and American magazines, London was one of the first American authors to become an international celebrity and earn a large fortune from writing. His most famous works, *The Call of the Wild* and *White Fang*, are set in [[Alaska]] and the [[Yukon]] during the Klondike Gold Rush. He also wrote the dystopian novel *The Iron Heel*, the nonfiction exposé *The People of the Abyss* and short stories such as "To Build a Fire." A member of the radical literary group "The Crowd" in [[San Francisco]], he was a passionate advocate of animal welfare, workers' rights and [[Socialism|socialism]]. He is reported to have been the first American writer to earn over a million dollars. He wrote about the South Pacific in stories such as "The Pearls of Parlay."

American actor and filmmaker, known for charismatic rebel roles. He won Academy Awards for Best Actor for *One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest* (1975) and *As Good as It Gets* (1997), and for Best Supporting Actor for *Terms of Endearment* (1983). His 12 Academy Award nominations are the most of any male performer. Notable roles include private investigator Jake Gittes in [[Chinatown (1974 film)|Chinatown]] (1974), the writer in *The Shining* (1980) and the [[Joker (character)|Joker]] in *Batman* (1989). He made his film debut in Roger Corman's *The Cry Baby Killer* (1958). He directed three films, including *Goin' South* (1978). He is one of only two actors nominated for acting in films from every decade from the 1960s to the 2000s, and he retired from acting after *How Do You Know* (2010).

American professional golfer and golf course designer, nicknamed "the Golden Bear." He won 117 professional tournaments, including a record 18 major championships. After winning the U.S. Amateur in 1959 and 1961, he turned professional in 1961 and won his first professional title at the 1962 U.S. Open, defeating Arnold Palmer in an 18-hole playoff. In 1966 he became the first player to win the Masters in back-to-back years, and at age 26 he was the youngest player to complete the career grand slam. He surpassed Bobby Jones's record of 13 majors. At age 46 he won his final major, the 1986 Masters, a record sixth Masters title. He captained the U.S. Ryder Cup team in 1983 and 1987 and won the Ryder Cup five times as a player. Through Nicklaus Design he has designed more than 425 golf courses, and he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2005.

Carved lantern, most commonly made from a pumpkin. Formerly made from a root vegetable such as a turnip or mangelwurzel, it is associated with [[Halloween]]. The name comes from lights flickering over [[Bog|peat bogs]], called will-o'-the-wisps. It may also have ties to the Irish legend of Stingy Jack, a drunkard doomed to roam the Earth with only a hollowed turnip to light his way. Carved pumpkins became a yearly Halloween tradition in the United States after Celtic-influenced immigrants brought carving customs. The top is cut off, the flesh scooped out and a face carved into the rind, and a candle or tealight is placed inside.

Unidentified [[Serial killer|serial killer]] active in the impoverished Whitechapel district of London's East End in 1888. Attacks typically involved women working as [[Prostitution|prostitutes]], whose throats were cut before abdominal mutilations. The removal of internal organs from at least three victims led to speculation about anatomical or surgical knowledge. The name originated in the "Dear Boss" letter, which is widely believed to be a hoax. The "From Hell" letter came with half a preserved human kidney, purportedly from one victim. A police investigation into eleven murders in Whitechapel and Spitalfields from 1888 to 1891 could not link all of them to the 1888 killings. The "canonical five" victims, killed between August 31 and November 9, 1888, are most often considered linked. The murders were never solved, and the legends have become a mix of historical research, folklore and pseudohistory.

Several [[Canidae|canid]] species native to [[Africa]] and [[Eurasia]]. In modern use the word refers mainly to the black-backed jackal and side-striped jackal of Central and Southern Africa, and the [[Golden jackal]] of south-central Europe and Asia. All jackals are opportunistic omnivores, predators of small to medium-sized animals and proficient [[Scavenger|scavengers]]. Their long legs and curved canine teeth suit hunting, and they can maintain speeds of 16 km/h (10 mph) over long distances. Jackals are crepuscular, most active at dawn and dusk. Their most common social unit is a monogamous pair that defends its territory by chasing intruders and marking landmarks with urine and feces. The English word dates to 1600 and derives from French *chacal*, from Ottoman Turkish *çakal*.

Fruit tree of the mulberry family (Moraceae), native to India. The evergreen *Artocarpus heterophyllus* can grow up to 30 m (98 ft) tall and bears the largest tree-borne fruit, up to 90 cm (35 in) long and weighing up to 50 kg (110 lb). The fruit grows from the trunk and large branches. Its yellowish flesh surrounds numerous seeds, and the bulbs and seeds are edible. Unripe fruit is cooked as a vegetable in curries and stir-fries, while ripe fruit is eaten fresh, canned or made into desserts. The species was first described by [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck]] in 1789. Its durable wood, resistant to [[Termite|termites]], is used for [[Furniture|furniture]] and [[Musical instrument|musical instruments]]. In traditional medicine across Asia, various parts of the tree are used.

[[Hong Kong]] martial artist, actor and filmmaker. Known for slapstick, acrobatic fighting and stunts he typically performs himself, Chan trained at the China Drama Academy and worked as a stuntman before acting. His breakthrough came with *Snake in the Eagle's Shadow* (1978). *Project A* (1983) established the Jackie Chan Stunt Team and his signature style of elaborate stunts combined with martial arts and slapstick. He became a Hollywood star as Chief Inspector Lee in *Rush Hour* (1998) and two sequels. Films in which he has appeared have grossed over $6 billion worldwide. He received an honorary Academy Award in 2016 and has stars on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] and the Hong Kong Avenue of Stars. In 2016 *Forbes* ranked him the second-highest-paid actor in the world.

American comedian and actor, known as "The Great One." He played bus driver Ralph Kramden in the television series *The Honeymooners*, and *The Jackie Gleason Show* maintained high ratings from the mid-1950s through 1970. He played Minnesota Fats in *The Hustler* (1961) and Buford T. Justice in the *Smokey and the Bandit* films. In the 1950s and 1960s he produced bestselling "mood music" albums. His first album, *Music for Lovers Only*, holds the record for the longest stay on the Billboard Top Ten charts, at 153 weeks. He received a nomination for an Academy Award, three Golden Globes and five Primetime Emmy Awards.

American [[Baseball|baseball]] player, the first African American to play in modern [[Major League Baseball]]. He broke the color line when he started at first base for the [[Brooklyn|Brooklyn Dodgers]] on April 15, 1947, ending the segregation that had relegated Black players to the Negro leagues since the 1880s. He was the inaugural National League Rookie of the Year in 1947 and an All-Star for six consecutive seasons. In 1949 he won the National League Most Valuable Player Award, the first Black player so honored. He played in six World Series and helped the Dodgers win the 1955 championship. He was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1962, in his first year of eligibility. His nonviolence and talent challenged segregation and contributed to the [[Civil rights movement|civil rights movement]]. In 1997 the league retired his uniform number 42 across all teams.

Capital and most populous city of Mississippi. Founded in 1821 as the new state capital and named for General [[Andrew Jackson]], the city sits on the Pearl River in the [[Deep South]]. Union forces under General William Tecumseh Sherman besieged and set fire to the city during the [[American Civil War|Civil War]] in 1863. Jackson surpassed Meridian as the state's most populous city during a natural gas boom in the 1920s. The city had 153,701 residents at the 2020 census, a decline of 11.42% since 2010. Its musicians have been prominent in [[Blues|blues]], gospel, folk and [[Jazz|jazz]], and its slogan is "The City with Soul."

American painter and major figure of the [[Abstract expressionism|abstract expressionist]] movement. He developed the "drip technique," pouring or splashing liquid household paint onto a horizontal canvas, which let him paint from all angles. Called all-over and action painting, his extreme abstraction divided critics. Reclusive and volatile, he struggled with [[Alcoholism|alcoholism]] for most of his life. In 1945 he married the artist Lee Krasner, who became an important influence on his career. He died in an alcohol-related single-car collision while driving. Four months later the [[Museum of Modern Art|Museum of Modern Art]] in New York City gave him a memorial retrospective, and larger retrospectives followed at MoMA in 1967 and, in 1998 and 1999, at MoMA and the Tate Gallery in London.
